newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO negotiators walk out of talks with Israel.
newsitem.headline: PLO negotiators walk out of talks with Israel.

text.p: Angry Palestinian negotiators walked out of peace talks with Israel late on Monday, describing the attitude of Israeli delegates as that of "occupiers toward the occupied."
The walkout followed an announcement by U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross that he was leaving for home, having failed in 15 days to achieve a breakthrough in Israeli-Palestinian talks on Hebron.

PLO security chief Mohammed Dahlan, referring to Israel's Dan Shomron, an ex-army chief, told Reuters: "Unfortunately the head of the Israeli delegation treats the Palestinian negotiators as if he is a military leader and not as a negotiator."

The two sides have held marathon sessions to close a deal on a long-promised Israeli troop pullout from Hebron, the last and most sensitive of seven West Bank towns due to be handed over to the Palestinians under a 1995 pact.
Both Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation have accused each other of stalling in the talks.
PLO officials said after the walkout that Shomron had insisted on discussing Israeli proposals already rejected by the Palestinians. Israeli officials were not immediately available for comment.
One PLO official said the Palestinian delegates had now gone to Bethlehem to brief Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on the talks.
Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy, speaking before the walkout, said the "other side...is in a situation of stretching out more time, that's it's own business."
But the PLO official, who declined to be identified, said a delay in reaching agreement was due to internal splits in the Israeli delegation, which includes both political and military negotiators.
Dahlan said earlier there was still no agreement on such major security issues as Israel's demand for a right of hot pursuit into areas due to be handed over to Palestinian police.

The Hebron handover has been held up since March, first by Islamic suicide bombings and then by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's concern for the security of 400 Jewish settlers living in enclaves in the heart of the town of 100,000 Arabs.

Dahlan said the Palestinians went to the negotiating table prepared to reach agreement quickly based on an accord reached with the previous Israeli governments of Shimon Peres and his slain predecessor Yitzhak Rabin.
"President Arafat wants to reach an agreement on redeployment in Hebron as soon as possible," he told Reuters.
